title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a model asserting fabricated information as fact, specifically a large language model generating nonexistent legal citations, incorrect case titles, and invented quotations that were then submitted in court filings. The failure occurred at the point of use: an attorney employed an AI tool under a mistaken belief about how it worked, assuming it was integrated with a vetted legal research service that included accuracy checks. That assumption was not correct, and no independent verification of the cited cases was performed before the filings were submitted.

The failure would have been caught by a routine step that legal practice already requires, checking that cited cases exist and that quotations match the actual text. Seven fabricated citations across eight filings went undetected by the lawyers who submitted them and were identified instead by opposing counsel. The lead attorney acknowledged he was unaware AI had been used at all, which indicates the tool's involvement was not disclosed internally before the filings went out.

What is not established is whether any court has yet ruled on sanctions, whether the underlying insurance dispute has been resolved, or whether the AI tool itself was defective as opposed to being used outside the conditions for which it was designed.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated false legal cases, quotes, and rulings in court filings. The homeowner's attorney discovered seven nonexistent case citations across eight filings, along with incorrect case titles and fabricated quotes. The lawsuit involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, whose home in Carson became uninhabitable after a 2020 fire. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and State Farm allegedly delayed approvals, leaving the home unfinished. Meni-Siliga and her husband exhausted their savings, filed for bankruptcy, and lost the home to foreclosure.

One State Farm lawyer, Jacquelene Robinson, explained she used an AI tool called Irys, mistakenly believing it was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription with built-in accuracy checks. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and the plaintiff, accepting responsibility despite claiming he was unaware AI had been used. The case is scheduled for trial in October. The incident reflects a growing trend, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI, raising concerns about accuracy in legal filings.
